items.title: Fourth Court Rejects Insurers' No Surprises Act Litigation Campaign - HEALTH CARE un-covered
items.reason: This article directly addresses federal litigation challenging the No Surprises Act, reporting on a fourth court decision rejecting insurers' legal campaign against the law, which is core to the litigation track of the topic definition.
items.summary: A fourth federal court has rejected insurers' litigation efforts to challenge the No Surprises Act, continuing a pattern of judicial defeats for the insurance industry's legal campaign against the law. The decision reinforces judicial support for the federal balance-billing protections and the No Surprises Act framework. This outcome is significant for revenue-cycle teams as it removes another potential legal barrier to the Act's continued implementation and suggests the courts are unlikely to overturn or substantially weaken the balance-billing rules insurers had sought to eliminate.

items.title: Complete Health to pay $14.1M in Medicare Advantage coding misuse allegations settlement
items.reason: This is a CMS enforcement action against a Medicare Advantage payer involving claims-coding fraud allegations and a significant monetary settlement, which directly matches the rubric's coverage of payer enforcement, sanctions, and Medicare Advantage penalties.
items.summary: Complete Health has agreed to pay $14.1 million to settle Medicare Advantage coding-fraud allegations covering the period 2020–2023. The settlement resolves CMS charges that the company submitted hierarchical condition codes (HCCs) that lacked clinical validity and were not supported by medical records or documented treatment plans. This enforcement action affects Medicare Advantage insurers and their coding practices, and signals continued CMS scrutiny of diagnosis-code submission accuracy—a critical issue for revenue-cycle teams managing MA plan compliance and claim documentation standards.

items.title: City and Insurer to Pay $53 Million Over Retiree Copay Lawsuit - The City Reporter
items.reason: This reports a settlement involving an insurer paying $53 million in a retiree copay lawsuit, which is a payer litigation and enforcement action directly affecting claims processing and member billing practices.
items.summary: A city and an insurer have agreed to pay $53 million to settle a lawsuit brought by retirees regarding copay practices. The settlement addresses claims that the insurer improperly charged or managed copayments for covered services to retirees, typically a health plan member group. This settlement is material for revenue-cycle teams as it may reflect enforcement of copay compliance standards and could signal new requirements around copay calculation, application, and member communication that affect billing processes and collections.
